tagline: Turns calls on your existing number into CRM-ready notes, with desktop dictation.
verdictSummary: The desktop dictation half — a hotkey, streaming transcription, an LLM cleanup pass, pasted into whatever's focused — is a solved, one-sitting build with mature open-source equivalents to build from. The actual hero product is not that: live-transcribing phone calls on your existing number needs carrier call forwarding, a pooled telephony number, a real softphone integration, and a call-audio pipeline that can only be debugged against live calls — that's the half this build deliberately leaves out.
coreLoopDIY: A hotkey-triggered dictation tool: stream microphone audio to a real-time transcription service, run one LLM cleanup pass, and paste the result into whatever app has focus.
whatYouLose: call capture on your existing phone number
auto-filing of dictations and calls to the right project or client
a searchable workspace of transcripts with reports and CRM drafts
Windows support and signed auto-updating installers
whyPeopleStillPay: People pay for the phone rail — answering calls normally on the number they already have, no separate app or device — and for everything downstream landing pre-organized: transcripts matched to the right client and turned into searchable history and CRM-ready notes without manual filing.
notes: Half of this is a clean, buildable dictation tool; the existing-number phone-call capture is the half that pulls the whole verdict down to 'kinda'.
prompt:
Build a push-to-talk dictation tool for macOS: a global hotkey held down records the microphone, streamed in real time to a speech-to-text API, showing partial results in a small floating panel as you speak. On release, run one LLM cleanup pass over the final transcript — fixing punctuation, dropping filler words — then paste the result into whatever field has focus, restoring the previous clipboard contents afterward. If no API key is configured for the real-time transcription service, fall back to recording locally and transcribing with a local Whisper model once you stop talking — slower, but fully offline and free. Keep a history of recent transcripts in a simple list with copy buttons.

Do not build live word-by-word typing into the focused field (paste on release is the honest, achievable version), Windows support, or — most importantly — the phone-call capture product: forwarding calls from your existing number needs carrier-level call forwarding and a telephony integration that's real infrastructure, not a weekend feature, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest about the scope. If call notes matter, upload a recording by hand instead.

faq.q: Can I bring over my Superscribe dictation history?
faq.a: There's no structured export of past dictations — this build starts its own local history from scratch, though nothing about your workflow otherwise changes.

faq.q: Will it work on my phone?
faq.a: The dictation tool itself is a macOS menu-bar utility tied to system-wide hotkeys, so no. And the phone-call capture feature this doesn't replace wouldn't run on the phone either — it works by forwarding calls to separate infrastructure.

faq.q: What does it cost to run?
faq.a: The real-time transcription API costs a small amount per use; falling back to the offline local model costs nothing beyond your own machine.

faq.q: What's the one thing that doesn't survive the rebuild?
faq.a: Calls on your existing phone number. That needs carrier call forwarding into a real telephony pipeline — genuine infrastructure this build deliberately doesn't attempt, not a missing feature that got cut for time.
